title: Gratitude with Jesus
subtitle: A thankful heart in the footsteps of Christ
author: Readalong Originals
description: A gentle, Scripture-rooted journey through gratitude in the life and teaching of Jesus, with simple practices for receiving grace and giving thanks in every season.

chapters.title: The One Who Came Back
paragraphs: The Gospel of Luke tells a story that is easy to pass over. Ten men with leprosy stood at a distance and called out to Jesus for mercy. In that time, leprosy meant isolation. It meant being cut off from family, worship, and ordinary life. These men were not simply sick. They were separated.

Jesus saw them and told them to go and show themselves to the priests. As they went, they were healed. All ten of them. The impossible thing happened on the road, in the middle of obedience, before any of them had time to arrange a proper thank-you.

One of them turned back. Luke says he came back praising God in a loud voice, threw himself at the feet of Jesus, and thanked him. And Luke adds a detail that stings: he was a Samaritan. The outsider was the one who returned.

Jesus asked the question that still hangs in the air: were not ten cleansed? Where are the other nine? The point is not that God withholds blessing from the ungrateful. The nine were still healed. The point is that gratitude sees what has happened and responds. It turns around. It comes back. It falls at the feet of the giver.

This is where the life of gratitude with Jesus begins. Not with a technique, but with a turning. We notice that we have been given something we could not give ourselves, and we come back to say so. The returning is not a payment. It is a relationship.

chapters.title: He Gave Thanks Before the Bread
paragraphs: In the Gospel of John, a huge crowd follows Jesus into a remote place. Thousands of people, far from home, with no food. The disciples look at the problem and see impossibility. Jesus looks at the crowd and sees people who need to be fed.

He takes the small offering that is available: five barley loaves and two fish. And before anything has changed, before the food has multiplied, before the crowd is seated, Jesus gives thanks. John says he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them.

That order matters. Thanksgiving came before the provision was visible. Jesus did not wait until the baskets were full to thank the Father. He received what was in his hands, acknowledged it as a gift, and trusted the giver with what would come next.

Most of us live the other way around. We plan to be grateful when the problem is solved, when the money arrives, when the diagnosis is clear, when the relationship is healed. Gratitude becomes a reward for good news. Jesus shows a different rhythm: gratitude as the posture we take while we are still waiting.

This does not mean pretending that the need is small. The crowd was hungry. The disciples were right about the size of the problem. But gratitude is not blind to the need. It simply refuses to let the need be the only thing in the room. It takes what is present, gives thanks for it, and opens a hand for more.

chapters.title: The Prayer That Begins with Thanks
paragraphs: Jesus prayed constantly. He withdrew to lonely places, he prayed before major decisions, and he taught his friends to pray. When they asked him, teach us to pray, he gave them a pattern that begins with relationship and reverence: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.

At the heart of that prayer is a posture of receiving. Daily bread is asked for, not earned. Forgiveness is requested, not purchased. Deliverance is trusted, not controlled. The Lord's Prayer assumes that we come to God as people who need things, which is another way of saying that we come as people who have something to be thankful for.

The early church took this posture into its central meal. They called it the Eucharist, a word that means thanksgiving. Before the bread was broken and the cup was shared, they gave thanks. Thanksgiving was not an extra song before the main event. It was the way the church learned to receive the gift.

For Jesus, prayer and gratitude were not separate activities. To pray was to stand before the Father with open hands. To give thanks was to name what those hands had already received. The two movements belong together: here is what I need, and here is what you have already given.

You can try this in your own prayer. Before you list your requests, name three things you have received today. Do not rush past them. Let the first movement be gratitude, and then let the second movement be need. You may find that the needs look different when they are held in grateful hands.

chapters.title: Gifts You Did Not Earn
paragraphs: Jesus told a parable about a landowner who hired workers at different hours of the day. Some worked all day in the heat. Others were hired at the eleventh hour and worked only one hour. At the end of the day, everyone received the same wage.

The workers who had labored longest were angry. It was not fair. And from a certain angle, they were right. But the landowner's answer cuts to the heart of grace: friend, I am not treating you unjustly. I am giving you what we agreed. Are you envious because I am generous?

Gratitude with Jesus is built on the discovery that we are not the all-day workers we imagine ourselves to be. We are people who have received far more than we earned. Grace is not a reward for good behavior. It is a gift that comes to us because God is good, not because we have earned the right to stand in line.

This is hard for anyone who has been taught to measure themselves by output. Comparison is the enemy of gratitude. When we are busy comparing our wage to someone else's, we cannot see the gift in our own hands. The parable does not say that everyone worked the same amount. It says that everyone was given more than they deserved.

Receiving grace does not make us lazy. It makes us free. A person who knows they are loved as a gift does not have to prove their worth by working harder than everyone else. They can work from gratitude instead of for it. That is a different kind of life.

chapters.title: Thanksgiving in the Dark
paragraphs: On the night before he died, Jesus went to a garden to pray. Matthew tells us he was sorrowful and deeply distressed. He did not give a brave speech. He said, my soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death. Then he fell on his face and asked the Father to let the cup pass from him.

This is the same Jesus who gave thanks before the bread. The same Jesus who taught his friends to trust the Father. And here he is, in agony, asking for another way. If gratitude were the same as pretending, Jesus would have failed the test. He did not pretend.

What he did was stay in the presence of the Father while the pain was real. He prayed honestly. He asked for what he wanted. And then he said, nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt. That nevertheless is one of the bravest words in Scripture. It does not erase the grief. It places the grief inside a larger trust.

Gratitude in the dark is not a cheerful denial of suffering. It is the choice to remain in relationship with God when the circumstances are not good. It is the prayer that says, I do not understand this, and I am still here. It is the small, stubborn act of thanking God for what has not been taken, while grieving what has.

If you are in a dark season, do not force a song. Jesus did not. Bring your honest lament. Bring your fear. Bring your questions. And when you are ready, look for one small sign of the Father's presence and thank him for it. That is enough for tonight. The garden did not last forever, and neither will this.

chapters.title: The Table of Thanksgiving
paragraphs: The night before he was betrayed, Jesus sat at a table with his friends. He knew one would betray him, one would deny him, and all would scatter. He knew what was coming. And still, he took bread.

He gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, this is my body, which is given for you. Then he took the cup, gave thanks, and said, this cup is the new covenant in my blood. Thanksgiving was not incidental to the Last Supper. It was the first thing he did with the bread and the cup.

The table became the place where the church learned to remember. When we gather around communion, we do what Jesus did: we receive, we give thanks, we break, and we share. The meal is a rehearsal of grace. It says that our life is not built on what we have achieved, but on what has been given.

Tables are also where gratitude becomes social. Jesus ate with tax collectors, sinners, Pharisees, and friends. He did not wait for people to become worthy before he sat down with them. At his table, people were seen, welcomed, and fed. Gratitude that stays private can become small. Gratitude that comes to a table tends to become love.

Who is at your table? Who has fed you, literally or spiritually? Who have you invited to eat with you? The practice of thanksgiving is not only words before a meal. It is the decision to make room for others at the meal. A thankful heart becomes a hospitable life.

chapters.title: Paul's Strange Command
paragraphs: Paul wrote to a young church in Thessalonica: rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks. It is a beautiful sentence, and a difficult one. In everything? Not just in the good things? Not just on the easy days?

It helps to notice what Paul does not say. He does not say give thanks for everything, as if every tragedy were secretly a blessing. He says in everything. The gratitude is not commanded toward the pain itself. It is commanded in the middle of the pain, alongside it, as a way of staying connected to God when life is falling apart.

Paul was not writing from a comfortable place. He knew shipwreck, beatings, imprisonment, and hunger. His command was not the advice of someone who had never suffered. It was the testimony of someone who had learned that gratitude is not dependent on circumstances. It is dependent on the character of the one who gives.

In his letter to the Philippians, Paul says, be careful for nothing; but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. Notice the order again. Prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving. The request and the thanks travel together. We do not wait for the answer to give thanks. We give thanks while we ask.

This is a practice, not a mood. It is built through repetition, on good days and bad. The more often we turn toward God in thanks, the more natural the turning becomes. Paul's strange command is not a burden. It is an invitation to a life that is not ruled by the weather.

chapters.title: The Ministry of Noticing
paragraphs: Jesus was always noticing people no one else noticed. He saw the widow putting two small coins into the temple treasury while the crowd watched the wealthy give large amounts. He did not praise the size of the gift. He praised the size of the sacrifice. He saw what she gave, not just what she had left.

He noticed children when his disciples tried to shoo them away. He noticed Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, when the crowd told him to be quiet. He noticed the woman at the well, with her complicated history, and spoke to her with truth and dignity. He noticed the man born blind, the tax collector in the tree, the servant whose ear was cut off.

Noticing is the first act of gratitude toward another person. To notice someone is to say, you are here, and you matter. Jesus did not treat people as background characters in his own story. He treated them as people worth seeing.

This has a social dimension. Gratitude is not only a private exercise in positivity. It is a way of honoring the people whose labor and love hold up our lives. The person who cleans the building. The driver who waits. The friend who remembers. The stranger who is kind. When we notice them, we are practicing the kind of attention Jesus practiced.

It also has a justice dimension. The people Jesus noticed were often the ones society overlooked. Gratitude that only notices the comfortable is not yet the gratitude of the Gospel. The thankful heart learns to see the lowly, the forgotten, and the ones who have no one to thank them. Sometimes the most grateful thing we can do is to make someone else visible.

chapters.title: When Gratitude Costs Something
paragraphs: Gratitude is not always a warm feeling. Sometimes it is an action that costs us something. In the Gospel of John, Mary of Bethany anointed the feet of Jesus with expensive perfume and wiped them with her hair. Judas objected that the perfume could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Jesus defended her.

We do not know everything that was in Mary's heart, but we know what her action looked like. It was extravagant. It was public. It was costly. She did not give Jesus a polite thank-you. She gave him something she could not easily replace.

Gratitude becomes real when it moves from words to offering. The widow gave her last coins. The Good Samaritan gave his time and money to a stranger. Jesus himself gave his life. In each case, gratitude or compassion was not just a feeling. It was a transfer of value from the one who had received to the one who needed.

This does not mean that we must always give away everything. It means that gratitude has a direction. It moves outward. It does not stay curled around itself. When we truly receive grace, we become more generous, more willing to share, more ready to give someone else a place at the table.

What would costly gratitude look like for you? Maybe it is a generous gift to someone in need. Maybe it is time you have been reluctant to give. Maybe it is a difficult act of service. Maybe it is simply speaking up for someone who is being ignored. Gratitude that costs something is gratitude that has become love.

chapters.title: A Thankful Life
paragraphs: The goal of this book is not to make you feel guilty about the times you forgot to say thank you. The goal is to invite you into a life that is increasingly shaped by gratitude. That life is not built in a day. It is built in small, repeated turnings toward the giver.

One practice is the daily examen. At the end of the day, look back over the last twenty-four hours and ask two questions: where did I receive something good today, and where did I give thanks? Do not judge yourself. Just notice. The examen is not a test. It is a way of learning to see.

Another practice is a thanksgiving walk. Walk for ten minutes with no destination, and name what you see: the sky, the trees, the people, the sounds. Let the walk become a prayer. You do not have to say anything complicated. A simple thank you is enough.

A third practice is the table. Before you eat, pause. Name the hands that grew, prepared, and served the food. Name the people who are with you. Give thanks for what is in front of you. This small ritual can change the way a meal feels, and it can teach a household to receive together.

Finally, remember the one who came back. The Samaritan did not return because he had earned his healing. He returned because he had received it. That is the whole story of gratitude with Jesus. We are not thanking God to secure a blessing. We are thanking God because the blessing has already come, and we have been invited to turn around and see it.

So go back to the feet of Jesus. Bring your thanks, your questions, your grief, and your small offerings. He is not asking for a perfect performance. He is asking for a thankful heart, one that notices, receives, and returns.
